records.name: Imo
records.current_summary:
Imo combines community violence with active state policing against gay people. In April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them; a follow-up report records that police took the two men in custody. In February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law, citing its 14-year term — the command's briefing expressly framed the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'.

The pattern runs across years and across modalities: mob justice met without accountability in 2018, and named, state-command enforcement invoking the criminal law in 2025. For a discovered visitor here, risk comes from neighbours and police alike.

sources.claim: 76crimes (26 Apr 2018): two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets accused of gay sex; a NoStringsNG inquiry found the victims were themselves arrested by police and may need legal support. Documents community vigilantism plus police processing of the accused.

Nigerian Newspoint (19 Feb 2025): Imo Police Command foiled a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels, Orogwe (Owerri West), arrested many gay and lesbian suspects, with fleeing attendees on a police search list. Evidence of active 2025 police enforcement against same-sex gatherings in Imo.

records.name: Aceh
records.current_summary:
Aceh is the only province in this country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own: the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) criminalises same-sex conduct (liwath, musahaqah) and close proximity (khalwat), with public caning as its signature punishment, applied by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside the secular Satpol PP units. Enforcement is active and widening: in August 2025 a Sharia court — sitting behind closed doors — sentenced two men to 80 strokes each for hugging and kissing, caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day; up to 100 strokes are available for morality offences generally, and Amnesty International called the practice 'state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty'.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them: a February 2025 boarding-house round-up detained a waria and a gay student facing up to 100 strokes under the liwath provision, with officials urging landlords to police tenants; in January 2018 police detained twelve transwomen and shaved their heads to teach them 'how to act like real men'. Private consensual conduct that carries no criminal penalty in any other province here can be publicly caned by a court in Aceh.

sources.claim: QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405): 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement' by UIN Ar-Raniry scholars (keywords: Law Enforcement, Waria, Aceh, Islamic Law, Qanun). Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens — the academic counterpart to the record's enforcement claims.

CBS News/AP (26 Aug 2025): two men were publicly caned in conservative Aceh province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing — the documented Aug-2025 caning episode the record's summary is built on, confirming public caning as the province's signature punishment.

iNews Aceh (undated local report, Feb-2025 round-up context): Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah Banda Aceh secured an alleged gay couple in a boarding house; a local advocate urged police to investigate and boarding-house owners to monitor tenants. Supports the record's Feb-2025 enforcement-reaches-trans-people claim.

UNSW Human Rights Research Centre: transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility; underpins this record's Indonesia-wide trans-violence context including the Jan-2018 twelve-transwomen detention claim that no Aceh-specific source in this record covers (rule-5 keep).

records.name: Lampung
records.current_summary:
In November 2018, Satpol PP (the regional moral-and-order force) raided three transwomen in Lampung, an incident the comparative UNSW/Harvard review of violence against Indonesian transwomen records as police-perpetrated violence. Lampung is also among the eight provinces identified in OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study as having discriminatory regional regulations. No further incidents, arrests, or enacted local bylaws specific to Lampung were found in the dossier period.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.02, at the minimum threshold. A single 2018 police raid on three transwomen is not a patterned campaign, and per the enforcement-over-statute rule, an OutRight-identified regulatory divergence without incident documentation is a small factor. The deviation is included because Lampung sits in the Sumatran belt where local Satpol PP enforcement against trans people is consolidating (alongside West Sumatra, South Sumatra, and North Sumatra).

Lampung is marginally above South Sumatra (0.13) in practical terms—both have one documented incident or announcement—but shares the same score due to equivalent evidence weight. It sits well above West Java (0.08), where a documented wave of ten attacks with 45 victims and zero prosecutions shows what unchecked local hostility looks like in operation.

sources.claim: UNSW human-rights review of anti-trans violence in Indonesia: documents that in November 2018 three transwomen were raided by Satpol PP (the regional morals-and-order force) in Lampung province — detained at the Satpol PP office and hosed down at the firefighter building, with an officer recording it — alongside a national pattern of transwomen murdered in 2017 (Bone, Semarang, South Sulawesi) and election-cycle anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying from 2016 onward; an SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians (Nov 2016) found LGBT people hated by 16.6%.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study analyses discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta — at province and district level; Lampung is named among them, supporting this record's claim of discriminatory regional regulation. (Text recovered by partial PDF extraction; cached file is a truncated PDF.)

freshness_all.fact: Same: national penal code effective Jan 2026 plus 2026 designation of 'LGBTQ+ culture spread' as a societal threat supersede the 2022 regional-drafting snapshot for this province.

records.name: West Papua
records.current_summary:
West Papua shares the same security-force pattern documented for Papua province: 138 recorded acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military (Sep 2021–Q1 2025) with near-total impunity, arbitrary airport detentions, expanded military deployments, and forced displacement through Q3 2025. No trans-specific incident series was identified. The risk to a trans visitor is amplification of any police contact into unlawful detention and physical violence at rates far exceeding the national norm.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.04. Like Papua, this is classified as a systemic-contact amplifier rather than a targeted-trans finding. The dossier explicitly notes the absence of trans-specific incidents while confirming that the probability of escalation during state contact is documented and elevated. West Papua's 2022 split from Papua means the same security apparatus operates under the same impunity conditions in the western portion of the island.

West Papua scores identically to Papua (0.11) and sits below the enacted-regulatory provinces West Sumatra (0.12) and South Sulawesi (0.12), where the risk is administrative or legislative rather than physical-state violence, and below Jakarta (0.12), where police overreach drew strong rights-group condemnation.
records.current_outOfScope: The general armed conflict between Indonesian security forces and TPNPB separatist groups, with its civilian casualties and displacement, is a security hazard for every traveller to the highlands regardless of gender expression; what matters for trans risk is the documented torture-in-detention and arbitrary-stop pattern that amplifies any contact with police.

sources.claim: Asia-Pacific Solidarity Network report (22 Jul 2025): police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands areas of West Papua committed 138 recorded acts of torture or other ill-treatment against people in detention (period through early 2025); most victims male under 24, seven female, seven minors aged 15-17, with near-total impunity — 'impunity, secrecy and silence'. Direct security-force risk context for any visitor to the province.

Papua human-rights monitor quarterly, Q3 2025: notable increase in military deployments and operations in West Papua's highland regions since August 2025; in Sorong police arrested over a dozen protest participants (Aug 2025); on 27 September 2025 a military task force opened fire on civilians in Agats, Asmat Regency; ongoing displacement and racial tension affecting indigenous Papuans. No trans-specific findings — risk relevance is the general security-force pattern amplifying exposure for any visibly gender-nonconforming visitor.

records.name: Central Kalimantan
records.current_summary:
Central Kalimantan is listed in the dossier among the provinces with no sub-national signal: no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found, and the province is NOT one of the eight identified in OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis of discriminatory regional regulations (that list covers Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta).

For a visitor, Central Kalimantan therefore tracks the national baseline: the KUHP criminal code in force from 1 January 2026 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide, and ordinary Sumatran/Java-style local moral policing is absent here — but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction. Any risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.

sources.claim: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa, 2022): mapping of national laws and regional regulations violating rights of women and LGBTIQ people in Indonesia; its eight-province list of discriminatory regional regulations does NOT include Central Kalimantan, which is the basis for treating the earlier 'one of the eight provinces' attribution for this unit as a misplacement of East Kalimantan.

sources.title: 2023 Indonesian Penal Code – Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and that because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline a visitor in Central Kalimantan stands under, consistent with this record's finding that the province's risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.

freshness_all.fact: 2022 regional-criminalisation landscape overtaken by the new national penal code in force Jan 2026 (cohabitation/extramarital acts), HRW World Report 2026 and a Jul 2026...

records.name: North Sumatra
records.current_summary:
North Sumatra is one of the eight provinces whose regional regulations OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study examined as discriminatory toward women and LGBTIQ people, including rules touching sexual orientation and gender expression. No specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted local bylaw targeting transgender people was documented in the dossier for this province. The signal is legal divergence without operational evidence.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.02, the minimum reporting threshold; the OutRight finding is a real but small factor absent enforcement documentation, and among the study's eight provinces the same no-incident profile appears in Yogyakarta.

For context, provinces with operational enforcement sit lower - Aceh (0.03) and West Java (0.08), and West Sumatra (0.11) with its enacted LGBT-targeting bylaws - while the capital territory, also an OutRight focus province, currently scores higher (0.16), and Bali 0.22. No sibling-specific violence or bylaw evidence elevates or depresses North Sumatra further.

sources.claim: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: The first but not the last: Indonesian transgender man fights for recognition | UNAIDS
sources.claim: Dimas Cahya, a transgender man from Medan (North Sumatra's capital), described to UNAIDS how he became the first transgender man in Medan to legally change his name to match his identity: after a six-week process the Medan District Court granted the application, and the judge, though warning the change would 'erase my identity', stayed out of LGBTI issues completely. The article frames Medan as conservative, with LGBTI people deemed 'immoral', and reports that a Medan legal-aid organisation asked the couple invasive questions before the case. For this record it is North Sumatra's only documented legal-process data point: a local court handled a trans person's application neutrally and no enforcement action against the couple is recorded anywhere in the article.

records.name: North Sulawesi
records.current_summary:
OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study examined regional regulations in eight provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - and North Sulawesi is not among them: the Sulawesi entry in the eight is South Sulawesi (the Makassar bylaw province), a different province. No enforcement incident, raid, arrest, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people was found in the dossier for North Sulawesi; the earlier attribution of an OutRight finding to this province was a misreading.

The recorded −0.02 deviation from the national score (0.15) was carried on that misattributed legal-divergence flag; the dossier contains no provincial evidence that would move North Sulawesi away from the national framework. A visitor-facing risk profile follows the national picture: the new KUHP code in force January 2026, and police extortion/arbitrary detention as the main mechanism.

North Sulawesi sits far above Aceh (0.03) and West Java (0.08), above West Sumatra (0.11), and below the capital territory (0.16) and Bali (0.22).

sources.claim: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: LGBT Manado Aksi Tolak Kekerasan Seksual - SuaraKita
sources.claim: On 11 June 2016 LGBT groups joined Manado's women's movement in a street action against sexual violence at Bundaran Zero Point, Manado, from 08.00 to 10.00 WITA; SALUT (Sanubari Sulawesi Utara), the local LGBT organisation whose director Coco Jericho was quoted, took part. The article records that police raids in Manado have included harassment of LGBT people - a butch lesbian groped during a raid, per SALUT - and that victims often do not report because of fear their families will not accept their orientation. It documents a public LGBT+ presence in Manado and a local account of raid-era conduct, with no arrests or prosecutions reported in the piece.

sources.title: Ketika Waria Berkontes Ratu Pantai - SuaraKita
sources.claim: On Saturday 10 November (2012) a waria beach-queen pageant was held at Malalayang beach, Manado, organised by Indonesian parliament member Paula Sinjal together with the National Narcotics Agency of North Sulawesi (BNN) as an outreach event on the dangers of drugs and HIV/AIDS. The report quotes Sinjal saying waria are among local people and deserve attention. It documents official-level engagement with North Sulawesi's waria community through a public pageant - evidence of a visible, organised trans community in Manado - with no adverse official action recorded.

sources.title: Hari Paling Buruk Dalam Hidup Ratu Waria: Media yang Sensasional telah Hancurkan Hidupku - Konde.co
sources.claim: This Konde.co interview profiles Alexa, elected Ratu Waria Sulawesi Utara 2016-2018 at the Sahid Kawanua Hotel in Manado, who says that after her title she suffered discrimination from sensationalist media and the public, with her personal crisis peaking around 25 March 2019. The article confirms a visible trans-women community culture in North Sulawesi - an elected province-level waria queen in Manado - while documenting the media-stoked stigma that follows public visibility. No legal or police action appears anywhere in the account.

records.name: Southeast Sulawesi
records.current_summary:
OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study analysed discriminatory regional regulations in eight provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta. Southeast Sulawesi is not among them; the dossier records no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted bylaw targeting transgender people in this province, and its inclusion in an eight-province 'OutRight bloc' was a misattribution (South Sulawesi, a different province, is the Sulawesi entry in the study).

The −0.02 deviation from the national score (0.15) was recorded on the strength of the legal-divergence reading corrected above; on the dossier's evidence the province carries no provincial-level signal in either direction, and visitor risk follows the national framework.

Comparatively, Southeast Sulawesi sits above the violence/corporal-punishment and bylaw units (Aceh 0.03, West Java 0.08, West Sumatra 0.11) and below the capital territory (0.16) and Bali (0.22).

sources.claim: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: POTRET KEHIDUPAN GAY DI KOTA KENDARI | Jurnal Budaya Etnika (ISBI)
sources.claim: A qualitative study by Universitas Halu Oleo researchers, published in Jurnal Budaya Etnika Vol. 8 No. 2 (23 December 2024), describes gay life in Kendari, the capital of Southeast Sulawesi: gay groups in the city say same-sex orientation has partly been converted into an economically valued 'profession', and that after identifying as gay they become more introverted and careful about expressing their feelings to others. The study documents same-sex communities in Kendari living discreetly, with no enforcement incident, raid or local regulation reported in the article. For this record it is the only Southeast Sulawesi-specific community evidence found, and it does not alter the national-framework risk profile described in the record.
